title: Effects of biodiversity-rich community gardens on health and biological diversity in municipalities: The cluster randomized HEBEDI trial
summary:
City life is associated with numerous health risks including exposure to heat islands, loneliness and alienation from nature. Observational studies suggest that community gardens with high levels of biodiversity, including wildflower meadows or deadwood, can reduce health risks by reducing stress and loneliness, as well as promoting physical activity and contact with nature. However, scaling biodiversity-rich community gardens is currently held back by limited evidence on their effectiveness. HEBEDI therefore investigates the effects of biodiversity in community gardens on health and biodiversity in the surrounding urban area. 

For this purpose, we compare biodiversity-rich and conventional community gardens by  randomly allocating the two garden types on available garden plots. With this study design, it is possible to investigate the effects of biodiversity on health. We focus on physical, mental and social health as well as perceived and objectively assessed biodiversity. In addition, HEBEDI investigates the mechanisms underlying the observed effects and identifies barriers and beneficial contextual factors that influence the relationship between the use of community gardens and health. Based on the results, the project team is developing a practice-oriented concept to support the implementation of biodiversity-rich community gardens in municipalities.

As an intervention study, HEBEDI contributes to the fundamental understanding of the health effects of biodiversity and thus complements the results of many observational studies.
